docs.title: 0. Chapter thread (memorize these three sentences first)
docs.text:
1. The Internet can be viewed from two perspectives: nuts and bolts (hosts, switches, links, networks) and services (the infrastructure that provides communication services to applications).
  2. Data crossing the network = packet switching + layered encapsulation; each layer adds its own header, and routers process only up to the network layer.
  3. Performance is determined by delay, loss, and throughput; the four delay components, \(La/R\), and the bottleneck link are the core of the calculation questions.

Common question types in this chapter

Question type Typical phrasing What to prepare Concept Three elements of a protocol? Four categories of nuts-and-bolts components? Memorize definitions + give examples Comparison Packet switching vs circuit switching Start from “whether resources are reserved / whether statistical multiplexing is used” Calculation The four delays, \(La/R\), throughput, store-and-forward Remember formulas + unit conversion Layering Five layers / OSI seven layers, encapsulation, PDU Draw the diagram + explain what each layer does Short answer Why layering? Routing vs forwarding? Answer with “decomposing a complex system / local vs global”

docs.title: 1.1 The “nuts and bolts” view ★
docs.text:
Component Role Example Host / end system Runs network applications PC, phone, server, IoT Packet switch Forwards packets router, switch Communication link Transmits bits fiber, copper, radio, satellite Network Collection of devices, routers, links home network, campus network, ISP network
  • The Internet = network of networks.
  • Link rate = bandwidth / transmission rate (bps).
  • Packet = chunk of data; switches use store-and-forward.

docs.title: 1.2 The “services” view
docs.text:
• The Internet is the infrastructure that provides communication services to applications.
  • It provides a Socket API: applications hand their data to the network.
  • Services include: reliable transfer, best-effort delivery, secure transmission, and so on (provided by combinations of different protocols).

docs.title: 1.3 Protocol ★
docs.text:
Protocol definition: ① message format; ② the order of messages sent and received; ③ the actions taken when a message is sent or received.

  • Human protocol: ask “what's the time?” → the other person answers; network protocol: TCP connection request → SYN-ACK.
  • The three elements can be summarized as: syntax, semantics, timing.

Why protocols are needed: both sides must agree on “how things are represented, who speaks first, and what to do on receipt”, otherwise they cannot communicate.

docs.title: 2.1 Access networks ★
docs.text:
Type Structure / medium Rate / characteristics Cable (HFC) coaxial cable + fiber to the cable headend; shared up to 40 Mbps–1.2 Gbps downstream; 30–100 Mbps upstream DSL telephone twisted pair to the DSLAM / central office; dedicated 24–52 Mbps downstream; 3.5–16 Mbps upstream Home network cable/DSL modem + WiFi AP + router WiFi 54/450 Mbps; wired 1 Gbps Wireless WLAN 802.11b/g/n, base station / access point 11/54/450 Mbps; shared, subject to interference Cellular 4G/5G base station 10’s of Mbps (higher with 5G); wide coverage Enterprise Ethernet switch + router 100 Mbps / 1 / 10 Gbps; WiFi AP Data center high-bandwidth switches connect large numbers of servers 10s–100s Gbps

The slides do not cover FTTH; as a supplement: fiber to the home, high rate and low loss, but high deployment cost.

Shared vs dedicated:

  • Cable and WiFi are shared media; multiple users compete for them;
  • DSL is a dedicated line to the central office;
  • Enterprise networks usually have wired access to the desktop and WiFi coverage.

docs.title: 2.2 Physical media ★
docs.text:
Type Description Twisted pair (UTP) cheap, easy to install; rate varies with category / distance Coaxial cable cable TV / broadband; shared Fiber optic cable high speed, low error rate, immune to electromagnetic noise, long distance Wireless radio wireless, mobile; affected by environment / interference / distance
  • Guided media: signals propagate in solid media.
  • Unguided media: signals propagate freely, e.g., radio.

docs.title: 2.3 How a host sends packets
docs.text:
• The application message is broken into packets of length L bits.
  • Link transmission rate R bps.
  • Transmission delay: \(L/R\).
  • Switches store and forward: the entire packet must arrive (and be checked) before it can be transmitted on the next link.

Example: L=10 Kbit, R=100 Mbps → \(\tfrac{L}{R} = \tfrac{10^4}{10^8} = 0.1\ \text{ms}\) (the slide example).

docs.title: 3.1 Forwarding vs routing ★
docs.text:
Concept Scope What it does Forwarding local, per packet move arriving packets from the router's input link to the appropriate output link, based on the local forwarding table Routing global, paths run routing algorithms to determine the source-destination paths taken by packets

Analogy: forwarding is “reading the sign at an intersection to pick a direction”; routing is “planning the whole route in advance”.

docs.title: 3.2 Packet switching ★★
docs.text:
• Data is split into packets that travel independently; statistical multiplexing (sharing bandwidth on demand).
  • Store-and-forward: receive the entire packet before forwarding.
  • Queueing: arrival rate (in bps) > output rate → packets queue in the buffer; buffer full → packet loss.
  • Advantages: great for bursty data, high bandwidth utilization, no call setup.
  • Disadvantages: queueing delay, packet loss, and the need for reliable data transfer / congestion control.

Store-and-forward delay over two links (no queueing or processing):

\[ d = \frac{2L}{R} \]

docs.title: 3.3 Circuit switching ★★
docs.text:
• End-end resources (bandwidth / slots) are reserved when the call is set up, and dedicated for the duration of the call.
  • FDM: frequency division multiplexing, different frequency bands;
  • TDM: time division multiplexing, periodic time slots.
  • Advantages: bandwidth / delay guarantees, good for real-time voice.
  • Disadvantages: wasted when idle, slow call setup, low resource utilization.

docs.title: 3.4 Packet switching vs circuit switching: the classic example ★★
docs.text:
Scenario: 1 Gb/s link; each user sends 100 Mb/s when “active”; active 10% of the time.

  • Circuit switching: 100 Mb/s reserved per call → at most 10 users.
  • Packet switching: with 35 users, the probability that more than 10 are active at the same time is < 0.0004 → no congestion most of the time.
  • Conclusion: packet switching is more efficient for bursty data; but packet switching gives no hard guarantees, and delay / loss rise under congestion.

How this is calculated: binomial distribution, P(X > 10) with X ~ B(35, 0.1); the slides only ask you to understand the conclusion.

docs.title: 3.5 Internet structure: a “network of networks”
docs.text:
• Access ISP → regional ISP → tier-1 ISP;
  • IXP (Internet Exchange Point) lets ISPs interconnect;
  • Content provider networks (Google, Netflix, Akamai) run their own CDN / backbone to bring content close to end users;
  • Business relationships: transit (paid transmission), peering (peering link), multi-homing.

docs.title: 4.1 The four sources of delay ★★
docs.text:
\[ d_{\text{nodal}} = d_{\text{proc}} + d_{\text{queue}} + d_{\text{trans}} + d_{\text{prop}} \] Component Formula / determining factor Magnitude Processing delay d_proc check bit errors, look up the forwarding table typically < µs Queueing delay d_queue depends on the congestion level, \(La/R\) from 0 up to very large Transmission delay d_trans \(L/R\) (packet length / link rate) determined by packet length and bandwidth Propagation delay d_prop \(d/s\) (distance / propagation speed) determined by physical distance
  • Propagation speed \(s \approx 2\times10^8\ \text{m/s}\) (about 2/3 the speed of light in fiber / copper).
  • ⚠ Transmission delay ≠ propagation delay: the former is “pushing the bits onto the link”, the latter is “the signal traveling through the medium”.

Example: L=1000 bytes=8000 bits, R=100 Mbps, d=2000 km, s=2×10⁸ m/s. - \(d_{\text{trans}} = \tfrac{8000}{10^8} = 80\ \mu\text{s}\) - \(d_{\text{prop}} = \tfrac{2\times10^6}{2\times10^8} = 10\ \text{ms}\) - total delay ≈ 10.08 ms (propagation dominates).

docs.title: 4.2 Traffic intensity and queueing ★★
docs.text:
\[ \text{traffic intensity} = \frac{La}{R} \]
  • a: average packet arrival rate (packets/sec); L: packet length (bits); R: link bandwidth (bit transmission rate).
  • \(\tfrac{La}{R} \approx 0\): average queueing delay is small;
  • \(\tfrac{La}{R} \to 1\): average queueing delay grows sharply;
  • La/R > 1: more “work” arriving than can be serviced, so the queue grows without bound (in practice, packets are lost).

Example: L=1000 bytes=8000 bits, a=100 packets/sec, R=1 Mbps: \(\tfrac{La}{R} = \tfrac{8000\times100}{10^6} = 0.8\) → close to 1, queueing delay will be noticeable.

docs.title: 4.3 Packet loss
docs.text:
• Router buffers are finite; if the arrival rate to the link keeps exceeding the output rate → the buffer fills up → later packets are dropped.
  • A lost packet may be retransmitted, which makes congestion even worse.
  • Symptoms: application timeouts, lower throughput, delay jitter.

docs.title: 4.4 Throughput ★★
docs.text:
• End-end throughput = the rate of the bottleneck link:
\[ \text{throughput} = \min(R_s, R_c, \ldots) \]
  • If 10 connections (fairly) share backbone R, each connection's throughput ≈ min(R_s, R_c, R/10).
  • The bottleneck is usually the access link (R_s or R_c), not the core backbone.

Example: server upstream 2 Mbps, client downstream 10 Mbps, backbone 100 Mbps → throughput = 2 Mbps.

docs.title: 4.5 traceroute
docs.text:
• Send probes with TTL=1, 2, 3, ...; each router returns an ICMP time-exceeded message; measure the RTT hop by hop.
  • You can see the path, the delay of each hop, and loss / routing changes.

docs.title: 5.1 Why layering ★
docs.text:
• Decompose a complex system into manageable modules;
  • Each layer relies only on the services provided by the layer below, so a layer's implementation can evolve independently;
  • Easier standardization, interoperability, and teaching.

Cost: header overhead, information hiding between layers, and difficulty of cross-layer optimization.

docs.title: 5.2 The five-layer model vs the seven-layer OSI model ★★
docs.text:
Internet five layers OSI seven layers Function PDU Application Application / Presentation / Session application semantics, representation, sessions message Transport Transport process-to-process segment Network Network host-to-host, routing datagram Link Data Link neighboring nodes, framing frame Physical Physical bit transmission bit
  • OSI's Presentation / Session are handled by the application layer itself in the Internet.
  • The five layers are the model commonly used in teaching and engineering; OSI is the reference model.

docs.title: 5.3 Encapsulation ★★
docs.text:
Application:  M
Transport:    [H_t | M]                 segment
Network:      [H_n | H_t | M]           datagram
Link:         [H_l | H_n | H_t | M]     frame
Physical:     bit stream
  • Each layer adds its own header; the receiver decapsulates layer by layer.
  • Routers process up to the network layer; link-layer switches process up to the link layer.
  • Headers are “contracts between layers”: addresses, protocol numbers, length, checksums, and so on.

docs.title: 5.4 End-end vs hop-by-hop
docs.text:
• Transport layer: end-end (process-to-process), implemented only at the two ends.
  • Network layer: hop-by-hop routing; every router takes part.
  • Link layer: hop-by-hop (neighboring nodes).

docs.title: 6.1 Common threats
docs.text: Threat Description Malware viruses, worms, Trojan horses, botnets DoS/DDoS a flood of traffic / requests exhausts resources Sniffing packet capture on shared media / wireless Spoofing forge the source IP / MAC

docs.title: 6.2 Historical phases
docs.text:
• 1961–1972: early packet-switching principles, ARPANET;
  • 1972–1980: internetworking, the beginnings of TCP/IP;
  • 1980–1990: protocol standardization, DNS, NSFNET;
  • 1990s: commercialization, the Web, browsers;
  • 2005–: mobility, cloud, SDN, CDN, IoT.

docs.title: Example 1: The four sources of delay (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: L=1500 bytes, R=1 Gbps, link length 3000 km, s=2×10⁸ m/s, processing delay 10 µs, queueing delay negligible. Find the nodal delay.

Solution: - \(L = 1500\times8 = 12000\ \text{bit}\) - \(d_{\text{trans}} = \tfrac{12000}{10^9} = 12\ \mu\text{s}\) - \(d_{\text{prop}} = \tfrac{3\times10^6}{2\times10^8} = 15\ \text{ms}\) - \(d_{\text{proc}} = 10\ \mu\text{s}\) - \(d \approx 10\ \mu\text{s} + 12\ \mu\text{s} + 15\ \text{ms} = 15.022\ \text{ms}\)

Marking points: unit conversion (bytes→bits, km→m, ms/µs); propagation delay dominates.

docs.title: Example 2: Store-and-forward (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: packet length 10 Kbit, link rate 100 Mbps, 2 links (1 router), processing / queueing ignored. Find the end-end transmission delay.

Solution: - Per link \(\tfrac{L}{R} = \tfrac{10^4}{10^8} = 0.1\ \text{ms}\) - Store-and-forward over two links: \(\tfrac{2L}{R} = 0.2\ \text{ms}\)

Marking points: the router must receive the entire packet before forwarding; with three links it would be 3L/R.

docs.title: Example 3: Packet switching vs circuit switching (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: 1 Gb/s link, 100 Mb/s when a user is active, active 10% of the time. How many users can circuit switching support at most? Why can packet switching support 35?

Solution: - Circuit: \(\tfrac{1\ \text{Gb/s}}{100\ \text{Mb/s}} = 10\) users (reserved per user). - Packet: with 35 users, the number active at the same time is X~B(35,0.1); P(X>10) < 0.0004, i.e., the link capacity is not exceeded the vast majority of the time. - Conclusion: statistical multiplexing improves utilization, but under congestion there is queueing / loss.

docs.title: Example 4: Throughput (6 points)
docs.text:
Question: server upstream 10 Mbps, client downstream 100 Mbps, backbone 1 Gbps, 10 connections fairly sharing the backbone. Find the throughput of a single connection.

Solution: - Bottleneck = \(\min(10\ \text{Mbps}, 100\ \text{Mbps}, \tfrac{1\ \text{Gbps}}{10} = 100\ \text{Mbps})\) = 10 Mbps. - If the backbone were only 50 Mbps, then \(\min(10, 100, 5) = 5\ \text{Mbps}\).

docs.title: Example 5: Encapsulation (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: describe the encapsulation / decapsulation process for an application message going from host A to host B across one router.

Solution: 1. The application on A generates message M; 2. The transport layer adds H_t → segment; 3. The network layer adds H_n → datagram; 4. The link layer adds H_l → frame; the physical layer sends it; 5. The router receives the frame, decapsulates it up to the network layer, looks up the forwarding table, and re-encapsulates it into a frame for the next link; 6. B decapsulates layer by layer and finally hands M to the application.

Marking points: the header added by each layer, the router going only up to the network layer, B decapsulating layer by layer.

docs.title: Example 6: Traffic intensity (6 points)
docs.text:
Question: packet length 1000 bytes, arrival rate 200 packets/sec, link 10 Mbps. Find the traffic intensity and judge the queueing situation.

Solution: - \(L = 8000\ \text{bit}\); \(\tfrac{La}{R} = \tfrac{8000\times200}{10^7} = 1.6\). - > 1: the arrival rate exceeds the service rate, so the queue keeps growing → severe queueing / loss.

docs.title: 8. Common mistakes (where marks are most easily lost)
docs.text: Wrong statement Correct understanding Transmission delay = propagation delay transmission is \(L/R\) (pushing the bits), propagation is \(d/s\) (the signal traveling) Larger bandwidth means smaller propagation delay propagation delay depends only on distance / medium, not on bandwidth Throughput = link bandwidth throughput = rate of the bottleneck link, which may be far less than the bandwidth Packet switching is always better than circuit switching it is more efficient for bursty traffic; circuit switching is more suitable for real-time / guaranteed services Circuit switching “has no delay” it has propagation / transmission delay; it just has no queueing / congestion Routers process up to the application layer routers go only up to the network layer; switches up to the link layer Five layers = OSI seven layers the five layers are the Internet model; OSI has a presentation layer / session layer More layers is always better layering costs header / performance overhead; it is a tradeoff Delay is stable when \(\tfrac{La}{R}=1\) as →1 queueing delay grows sharply; at >1 the queue grows without bound A protocol only defines the message format it also defines the order / timing and the actions taken on receipt

docs.title: 9. Self-test (do it first, then check the answers)
docs.text:
1. From the “nuts and bolts” view, what four categories of components make up the Internet?
  2. What are the three elements of a protocol? Explain with the “asking the time” analogy.
  3. What is the core difference between packet switching and circuit switching? What are the pros and cons of each?
  4. Write out the four components of nodal delay; which of them depend on packet length?
  5. What happens as \(La/R\) approaches 1? Why?
  6. What is the difference between transmission delay and propagation delay? What determines each?
  7. What are the PDU names at each layer of the five-layer protocol stack? How does encapsulation work?
  8. What is the difference between routing and forwarding?
  9. Why layering? What does it cost?
  10. What is the difference between FDM and TDM in circuit switching?
  11. What determines end-end throughput? How do you compute it when 10 connections share the backbone?
  12. How does traceroute work?

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
1. Hosts / end systems, packet switches (routers / switches), communication links, networks (a network of networks).
  2. Message format, order / timing, and the actions taken after receiving a message; a human asks the time → an answer, a network request → a response.
  3. Packet: statistical multiplexing, good for bursty traffic, possible queueing / loss; circuit: reserved resources, guarantees, wasted when idle.
  4. Processing, queueing, transmission \(L/R\), propagation \(d/s\); transmission depends on packet length, propagation depends on distance / medium.
  5. Queueing delay grows sharply and buffer overflow causes packet loss; the arrival rate keeps exceeding the output rate.
  6. Transmission: pushing the bits onto the link, \(L/R\); propagation: the signal traveling through the medium, \(d/s\).
  7. Application message, transport segment, network datagram, link frame, physical bit; each layer adds its header.
  8. Routing: global path selection (routing algorithms); forwarding: locally moving packets from the input link to the output link.
  9. Decomposing a complex system, independent evolution of modules, standardization; the cost is header overhead and information hiding between layers.
  10. FDM divides frequency into bands; TDM divides time into slots; both reserve resources.
  11. The bottleneck link min(R_s,R_c,...); with 10 connections fairly sharing backbone R, each gets min(R_s,R_c,R/10).
  12. Send probes with increasing TTL, each router returns an ICMP time-exceeded message, and measure the RTT hop by hop.

docs.text: Point Content Four categories of components hosts, packet switches, links, networks Three elements of a protocol format, order, action Circuit switching reserved resources; FDM/TDM; the 10-user example Packet switching statistical multiplexing; store-and-forward; queueing / loss; the 35-user example Delay d_proc + d_queue + d_trans + d_prop Transmission / propagation \(L/R\); \(d/s\) Traffic intensity \(La/R\); →1 means large delay, >1 means loss Throughput min(R_s,R_c,...); 10 connections R/10 Five layers application / transport / network / link / physical PDU message/segment/datagram/frame/bit Encapsulation each layer adds a header; routers up to the network layer Routing vs forwarding global path vs local port

docs.title: Chapter 2 · Application Layer · Review Notes
docs.text:
Matching slides: ch2-8.pdf (Kurose & Ross, Chapter 2 Application Layer, 8th ed.)

Suggested time: first pass 90 minutes + worked examples 40 minutes + self-test 30 minutes

Companion: Outline §3

Weight of this chapter: HTTP (RTT / caching / HTTP2), DNS (hierarchy / resolution / RR), the P2P distribution formula, and socket programming are high-frequency exam points.

docs.title: 0. Chapter thread (memorize these three sentences first)
docs.text:
1. The application layer runs only on end systems: a process hands data to the transport layer through its socket; an application protocol defines message types, syntax, semantics, and timing.
  2. HTTP is a stateless request/response protocol; cookies add state and caches reduce delay; HTTP/2 solves multiplexing of multiple objects, and HTTP/3 uses QUIC to solve TCP head-of-line blocking.
  3. DNS is a distributed, hierarchical database: root → TLD → authoritative → local resolver; UDP 53; caching improves performance but entries expire / get poisoned.

Common question types in this chapter

Question type Typical phrasing What to prepare Calculation RTT of non-persistent / persistent HTTP; P2P vs C-S distribution time Remember the formulas + draw the timing diagram Procedure From URL to page display; DNS iterated / recursive query Chain it as “resolution → TCP → HTTP” Comparison HTTP/1.1 vs 2 vs 3; SMTP vs HTTP; C-S vs P2P Make a table of the key differences Mechanism cookies, caches, conditional GET, DASH, CDN Explain clearly “what problem it solves” Socket call order of the UDP/TCP client and server Remember socket/bind/listen/accept/connect

docs.title: 1.1 Two architectures ★
docs.text: Architecture Characteristics Advantages Disadvantages Examples Client-Server server always-on, permanent IP address, client initiates requests easy to manage, easy to scale (data centers) server bandwidth / single point of bottleneck Web, email, DNS P2P no always-on server; peers both request and provide service scalable, low cost complex management, churn, incentive problem BitTorrent

docs.title: 1.2 Processes, sockets, addressing ★
docs.text:
• Process: program running within a host.
  • Same host: process ID; across hosts: IP address + port number.
  • Socket: the interface between the application process and the transport layer (an API object).
  • The application hands messages to the socket; the transport layer delivers them to the destination socket.

An application-layer protocol defines:

  1. types of messages exchanged (request, response);
  2. message syntax (fields, format);
  3. field semantics;
  4. rules for when and how messages are sent and responded to (timing).

docs.title: 1.3 What transport service does an app need? ★
docs.text:
Requirement Description Typical applications Data integrity no loss / no errors file transfer, Web, email Timing low delay real-time audio/video, games Throughput minimum bandwidth streaming video Security encryption / authentication login, payment

Internet transport services

  • TCP: reliable, in-order, flow control, congestion control, connection-oriented; does not provide timing or minimum throughput guarantee.
  • UDP: unreliable, connectionless, low overhead; does not guarantee order or integrity.
  • TLS: provides encryption, authentication and data integrity on top of TCP; applications use it through TLS libraries (HTTPS).

docs.title: 1.4 Transport choices for common apps
docs.text: Application Transport Reason Web/HTTP TCP (or QUIC/UDP) needs reliability and in-order delivery File transfer TCP cannot lose data Email/SMTP TCP reliable DNS UDP (TCP when needed) short queries, low delay Streaming media TCP/UDP (DASH/QUIC) adaptive / low delay Real-time games / voice UDP better to lose packets than to wait

docs.title: 2.1 HTTP basics ★
docs.text:
• HTTP: hypertext transfer protocol; request/response model; stateless.
  • default port 80; uses TCP (HTTP/3 uses QUIC/UDP).
  • client: browser; server: Web server.

Two types of connections

Type Behavior Response time Non-persistent (HTTP/1.0) a new TCP connection per object, closed after use 2 RTT + file transmission time per object Persistent (HTTP/1.1) server leaves the connection open after sending; subsequent requests reuse it 1 RTT to set up the connection; then 1 RTT per object; with pipelining, “as little as one RTT for all the referenced objects”

RTT (definition): time for a small packet to travel from client to server and back (excluding the time to transmit the large file).

The RTT account of non-persistent HTTP:

  1. initiate TCP connection: one RTT;
  2. send the HTTP request and receive the first few bytes of the HTTP response: one RTT;
  3. object transmission time: \(L/R\). → per object 2 RTT + L/R.

Persistent HTTP:

  • server sends Connection: keep-alive;
  • the client can send multiple requests back to back;
  • without pipelining: one RTT per object; with pipelining: several requests are sent back to back, so all objects can arrive one after another after roughly one RTT.

docs.title: 2.2 HTTP messages ★
docs.text:
Request

GET /index.html HTTP/1.1\r\n
Host: www.example.com\r\n
User-Agent: ...\r\n
Accept: text/html\r\n
Connection: keep-alive\r\n
\r\n
  • request line: method, URL, version.
  • methods: GET, POST, HEAD, PUT, DELETE.
  • header lines: Host, User-Agent, Accept, Accept-Language, Connection, Cookie, etc.

Response

HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n
Date: ...\r\n
Server: ...\r\n
Content-Length: 1234\r\n
Content-Type: text/html\r\n
\r\n
(entity body)

Status codes

Code Meaning 200 OK 301 Moved Permanently (permanent redirect) 304 Not Modified (cached copy is up to date) 400 Bad Request 403 Forbidden 404 Not Found 505 HTTP Version Not Supported

docs.title: 2.3 Cookies ★★
docs.text:
Question: HTTP is stateless, so how does the server “remember” the user?

Mechanism:

  1. the server's response carries Set-Cookie: user=alice; ...;
  2. the browser stores the cookie (per domain / path);
  3. subsequent requests carry Cookie: user=alice;
  4. the server uses a back-end database to associate the user state.

Uses: shopping carts, sessions, personalization, tracking.

Risks: cross-site tracking, privacy; a cookie is “weak authentication” and cannot replace real authentication / authorization.

docs.title: 2.4 Web caches (proxy servers) ★★
docs.text:
• Cache: stores responses to recent requests; on a hit it returns the object directly without contacting the origin server.
  • Effects: reduce response time, reduce traffic on the access link, reduce the load on the origin server.
  • A cache acts as both client and server (proxy).

Conditional GET

  1. the cache has the object, but it may be out of date;
  2. it sends a request with If-Modified-Since: <date>;
  3. the object has not been modified at the server → 304 Not Modified (no entity body);
  4. the cache returns its local copy to the client.

Cache consistency: Cache-Control, Expires, ETag/If-None-Match.

Caching example (slides):

  • access link 1.54 Mbps, RTT 2 s, object 100 Kbit, request rate 15/s.
  • average data rate \(15\times100\text{K} = 1.5\ \text{Mbps}\) → utilization \(\tfrac{1.5}{1.54}\approx0.97\) → queueing delay of “minutes”.
  • Option 1: upgrade to 154 Mbps → utilization 0.0097, delay ~2 s + ms, but expensive.
  • Option 2: install a cache, hit rate 0.4 → only 60% of requests go over the access link → average 0.9 Mbps → utilization 0.58, delay ~2 s + ms, cheap.
  • Conclusion: caching is usually cheaper than upgrading bandwidth.

docs.title: 2.5 HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 ★
docs.text:
Problems with HTTP/1.1

  • one request/response at a time per connection (without pipelining);
  • multiple objects require multiple connections;
  • head-of-line (HOL) blocking: a large object blocks the small objects behind it;
  • repeated headers and a redundant text format.

HTTP/2

  • binary framing: messages are divided into frames;
  • multiplexing: multiple streams concurrently over one TCP connection;
  • header compression (HPACK);
  • still affected by HOL blocking at the TCP layer (lose one TCP segment and all streams wait).

HTTP/3

  • based on QUIC (UDP);
  • stream-level multiplexing: packet loss on one stream does not affect the other streams;
  • 0/1-RTT connection setup;
  • built-in TLS 1.3 encryption;
  • connection migration (phone switching networks).

docs.title: 3.1 Components
docs.text:
• User agent (UA): Outlook, phone mail app.
  • Mail servers: sender / receiver servers; maintain the user mailbox and the message queue.
  • SMTP: sends / forwards e-mail messages.
  • Mail access protocols: POP3, IMAP, HTTP (Webmail).

docs.title: 3.2 SMTP ★
docs.text:
• Push: sender UA → sender mail server → receiver mail server.
  • uses TCP port 25; commands / responses are ASCII.
  • procedure:
  • client HELO;
  • MAIL FROM;
  • RCPT TO;
  • DATA → message content → .;
  • QUIT.
  • SMTP is a “server-to-server” protocol; UA-to-server also uses SMTP (submission).

docs.title: 3.3 Mail access
docs.text: Protocol Port Characteristics POP3 110 simple download; usually delete / keep after download IMAP 143 server-side folders, read / unread state; multi-device synchronization HTTP 80/443 Webmail

docs.title: 3.4 Mail message format and MIME
docs.text:
• Header lines: From, To, Subject, Date, Cc, Bcc.
  • A blank line separates the header from the body.
  • MIME: supports non-ASCII text, attachments, multipart bodies; Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding.

docs.title: 3.5 SMTP vs HTTP
docs.text: Dimension SMTP HTTP Direction push (sender initiates) pull (client requests) Purpose e-mail transfer Web content Transport TCP 25 TCP 80 Format ASCII commands / responses text requests / responses

docs.title: 4.1 Services ★
docs.text:
• hostname-to-IP-address translation;
  • host aliasing (CNAME);
  • mail server aliasing (MX);
  • load distribution (multiple A records).

Why not centralize DNS: single point of failure, traffic volume, distant centralized database, maintenance.

docs.title: 4.2 Hierarchical structure ★★
docs.text:
Root DNS servers (root)
  → Top-Level Domain TLD (.com, .org, .cn, .edu)
    → Authoritative DNS servers (authoritative)
Local DNS server (local resolver, provided by ISP / organization)
  • Root: 13 logical clusters, replicated many times worldwide (~200 servers in the US); managed by ICANN.
  • TLD: responsible for .com/.org/.cn, etc.; returns the address of the authoritative server.
  • Authoritative: the organization's own DNS, holding authoritative hostname→IP records.
  • Local DNS: forwards queries, caches; usually provided by the ISP / school.

docs.title: 4.3 Name resolution process ★★
docs.text:
Iterated query

  1. the host asks its local DNS server;
  2. the local DNS server asks the root → the root returns the .com TLD address;
  3. the local DNS server asks the .com TLD → it returns the amazon.com authoritative address;
  4. the local DNS server asks the authoritative server → it returns the IP address;
  5. the local DNS server returns the result to the host and caches it.

Recursive query

  • the host asks the local DNS server to “resolve it completely on my behalf”; the local DNS server is responsible for all subsequent queries.
  • root / TLD servers usually do not do recursion (they only give the next hop).

In practice: host→local DNS is recursive; local DNS→root/TLD/authoritative is iterative.

docs.title: 4.4 Caching
docs.text:
• any name server can cache; TTL controls expiration.
  • Advantages: lower delay, less load on the root / TLD servers.
  • Disadvantage: cached entries may be out of date (“best-effort”).

docs.title: 4.5 Resource records (RR) ★
docs.text:
Type Meaning Example A hostname → IPv4 www.example.com → 1.2.3.4 NS authoritative DNS server for the domain example.com → dns.example.com CNAME alias name → canonical name www.ibm.com → servereast.backup2.ibm.com MX mail server for the domain example.com → mail.example.com AAAA (supplementary) hostname → IPv6 —

Format: (name, value, type, ttl).

docs.title: 4.6 DNS messages
docs.text:
• Header: 16-bit ID, flags, # questions, # answer RRs, # authority RRs, # additional RRs.
  • Four sections: questions, answers, authority, additional.
  • Query and reply messages have the same format; the ID is used to match request / response.

docs.title: 4.7 DNS security ⚔
docs.text:
Attack Description Defense DDoS bombard the root / TLD / authoritative servers, or send a flood of queries rate limiting, anycast, redundancy Cache poisoning forge a reply so that the cache stores a bogus record DNSSEC, randomized ID / port, 0x20 Spoofed reply guess the ID / port and answer first randomization, source port randomization DNS spoofing modify the local hosts / DNS configuration encrypted DNS, DNSSEC
  • DNSSEC: signs DNS records, providing authentication and message integrity (not confidentiality).

docs.title: 5.1 File distribution time ★★
docs.text:
Client-Server

\[ D_{\text{cs}} = \max\left\{\frac{NF}{u_s},\ \frac{F}{d_{\min}}\right\} \]
  • the server must upload N copies: \(\tfrac{NF}{u_s}\);
  • the slowest client's download: F/d_min.

P2P

\[ D_{\text{p2p}} = \max\left\{\frac{F}{u_s},\ \frac{F}{d_{\min}},\ \frac{NF}{u_s + \sum_i u_i}\right\} \]
  • the server must upload at least one copy: F/u_s;
  • the slowest client: F/d_min;
  • the total upload capacity of all peers: \(u_s + \sum u_i\), and \(NF\) bits must be distributed.

Conclusion: C-S grows linearly in N; the denominator for P2P grows with N, so P2P is scalable.

docs.title: 5.2 BitTorrent ★
docs.text:
• the file is divided into chunks of 256 KB.
  • tracker: tracks the peers participating in the torrent.
  • a peer joins: it asks the tracker for a list of peers and connects to a subset of neighbors.
  • requesting: rarest first (ask for the rarest chunks first).
  • sending: tit-for-tat:
  • re-evaluate every 10 seconds, preferring the 4 peers with the highest upload rate;
  • every 30 seconds “optimistically unchoke” one random peer, giving it a chance.
  • churn: peers may come and go at any time; once the download is complete a peer may leave or remain.

docs.title: 6.1 Video basics
docs.text:
• video = a sequence of images; compression exploits spatial / temporal redundancy.
  • CBR (constant bit rate) vs VBR (variable bit rate).
  • streaming challenges: the continuous playout constraint, network jitter, changing bandwidth.

docs.title: 6.2 Playout buffering
docs.text:
• the client pre-buffers a few seconds to absorb network jitter;
  • cost: start-up delay; a buffer that is too small → stalling, too large → high delay.

docs.title: 6.3 DASH
docs.text:
• Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP:
  • the video is divided into short chunks, each offered at multiple rates;
  • the client measures the bandwidth and chooses the rate on demand;
  • chunks are pulled over HTTP, which passes through NAT / firewalls easily.

docs.title: 6.4 CDN ★
docs.text:
• Content Distribution Network: places copies of content at edge nodes.
  • users are redirected by DNS / HTTP to the nearest / optimal node.
  • Advantages: lower delay, less backbone traffic, higher availability.
  • OTT: the content provider goes over the top of traditional operators and builds its own CDN / network (Netflix, YouTube).

docs.title: 7.1 UDP
docs.text:
Server

sock = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM)
sock.bind(('', port))
loop:
    data, addr = sock.recvfrom(2048)
    sock.sendto(reply, addr)

Client

sock = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM)
sock.sendto(msg, (server, port))
data, addr = sock.recvfrom(2048)
  • connectionless; sendto/recvfrom preserve datagram boundaries; packets may be lost or arrive out of order.

docs.title: 7.2 TCP
docs.text:
Server

sock = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM)
sock.bind(('', port))
sock.listen(5)
conn, addr = sock.accept()
conn.recv(1024)
conn.send(reply)
conn.close()

Client

sock = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM)
sock.connect((server, port))
sock.send(msg)
sock.recv(1024)
  • connection-oriented; byte stream with no message boundaries; you must delimit messages yourself (length prefix / newline).

docs.title: 7.3 UDP vs TCP sockets
docs.text: Dimension UDP TCP Connection none three-way handshake Boundaries preserved byte stream Reliability not guaranteed reliable / in-order Calls sendto/recvfrom connect/listen/accept/send/recv

docs.title: Example 1: HTTP RTT (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: RTT=100 ms, 10 objects, transmission time 1 ms per object. Find the total time for non-persistent HTTP, persistent HTTP (without pipelining) and persistent HTTP (with pipelining) (ignore DNS).

Solution: - Non-persistent: \(10\times(2\times100+1) = 2010\ \text{ms}\). - Persistent without pipelining: 100 ms to set up the connection + 10 × (100 + 1) = 1110 ms. - Persistent with pipelining: 100 ms to set up the connection + 100 ms for request / first bytes + 10×1 ms ≈ 210 ms. - Conclusion: persistent + pipelining greatly reduces RTT overhead.

docs.title: Example 2: Benefit of caching (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: access link 1.54 Mbps, object 100 Kbit, request rate 15/s, RTT 2 s. Find the utilization without a cache; if the cache hit rate is 0.4, find the utilization.

Solution: - average data rate \(15\times100\ \text{Kbit} = 1.5\ \text{Mbps}\); utilization \(\tfrac{1.5}{1.54}\approx0.97\) → high queueing delay. - cache hit 0.4 → only 60% go over the link → \(0.6\times1.5 = 0.9\ \text{Mbps}\); utilization \(\tfrac{0.9}{1.54}\approx0.58\) → delay drops significantly. - Conclusion: caching is more economical than upgrading bandwidth.

docs.title: Example 3: DNS query (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: www.example.com is not in any cache; describe the iterated query process.

Solution: 1. host → local DNS (recursive request); 2. local DNS → root: returns the .com TLD address; 3. local DNS → .com TLD: returns the example.com authoritative address; 4. local DNS → authoritative: returns the A record for www.example.com; 5. the local DNS caches it and returns it to the host.

docs.title: Example 4: P2P distribution (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: F=1 GB, u_s=10 Mbps, N=10, u_i=1 Mbps for each peer, d_min=10 Mbps. Find the distribution time for C-S and for P2P.

Solution: - \(F = 8\ \text{Gbit} = 8000\ \text{Mbit}\). - C-S: \(\max\{10\times8000/10,\ 8000/10\} = \max\{8000,800\} = 8000\ \text{s}\). - P2P: \(\max\{8000/10=800,\ 800,\ 10\times8000/(10+10)=4000\} = 4000\ \text{s}\). - P2P takes about half of C-S; the advantage grows with N.

docs.title: Example 5: Socket call order (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: write out the call order for a TCP server and client to set up a connection and exchange data.

Solution: - Server: socket → bind → listen → accept → recv → send → close. - Client: socket → connect → send → recv → close.

docs.title: 9. Common mistakes (where marks are most easily lost)
docs.text: Wrong Correct HTTP is a stateful protocol HTTP is stateless; cookies add state non-persistent HTTP costs 1 RTT per object 2 RTT + transmission time persistent HTTP has no RTT overhead at all 1 RTT to set up the connection; without pipelining 1 RTT per object; with pipelining about 1 RTT in total cookies are an authentication mechanism only state management, with very weak authentication power a cache always guarantees the latest version it may be out of date; conditional GET / 304 is needed DNS has only 13 physical servers 13 logical clusters, each replicated many times DNS queries are always recursive host→local is usually recursive; local→root/TLD is usually iterative SMTP is a pull protocol SMTP is push; POP3/IMAP are pull P2P is always faster than C-S it depends on the peers' upload bandwidth / number; the formula takes the max UDP has no checksum UDP has a 16-bit checksum (optional but usually enabled) TCP is a message-boundary protocol TCP is a byte stream, with no message boundaries HTTP/2 completely solves HOL blocking it only solves it at the HTTP layer; TCP-layer HOL blocking remains, and only HTTP/3 solves that

docs.title: 10. Self-test (do it first, then check the answers)
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between Client-Server and P2P? What are the pros and cons of each?
  2. What identifies a socket? How do the demultiplexing identifiers of TCP and UDP differ?
  3. How does the response time of non-persistent HTTP differ from persistent HTTP? How is RTT defined?
  4. How do cookies work? What HTTP problem do they solve? What privacy risks do they carry?
  5. What is the role of a Web cache? How does conditional GET work? What does 304 mean?
  6. What HTTP/1.1 problems does HTTP/2 solve? What does HTTP/3 solve in turn?
  7. How do SMTP and HTTP differ? Why does e-mail use push and the Web use pull?
  8. What is the hierarchical structure of DNS? What is the difference between iterated and recursive queries?
  9. What are the common DNS RR types and their meanings? What are the benefits and risks of DNS caching?
  10. What is the P2P file distribution time formula? Why is P2P scalable?
  11. How does a CDN reduce delay? How does DASH adapt to bandwidth?
  12. What are the main differences between UDP and TCP socket programming?

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
1. C-S: always-on server, easy to manage, server bottleneck; P2P: scalable, complex management, incentive problem.
  2. IP + port; UDP uses destination IP + destination port, TCP uses the four-tuple.
  3. Non-persistent: 2 RTT per object; persistent sets up once, then 1 RTT per object (with pipelining about 1 RTT in total); RTT is the round-trip time of a small packet.
  4. Set-Cookie / Cookie header + a server database; makes up for HTTP being stateless; cross-site tracking.
  5. Reduces response time / bandwidth / server load; If-Modified-Since; 304 means not modified.
  6. HTTP/2: binary framing, multiplexing, header compression, mitigating HTTP-layer HOL blocking; HTTP/3: QUIC/UDP, stream-level multiplexing, avoiding TCP HOL blocking.
  7. SMTP pushes, HTTP pulls; e-mail must be delivered to the receiver's mail server, while the Web client fetches actively.
  8. root→TLD→authoritative→local; with iteration you ask each server yourself, with recursion the contacted server resolves on your behalf.
  9. A/NS/CNAME/MX (+AAAA); caching lowers delay / load, but entries may be out of date / poisoned.
  10. max{F/u_s, F/d_min, NF/(u_s+Σu_i)}; peer upload bandwidth grows with N.
  11. edge copies, serving from a nearby node, less backbone traffic; DASH divides the video into chunks at multiple rates and the client chooses by bandwidth.
  12. UDP: connectionless, datagram boundaries, sendto/recvfrom; TCP: connection-oriented, byte stream, listen/accept/connect.

docs.title: Chapter 3 · Transport Layer · Review Notes
docs.text:
Matching slides: ch3-8.pdf (Kurose & Ross, Chapter 3 Transport Layer, 8th ed.)

Suggested time: first pass 120 minutes + worked examples 50 minutes + self-test 40 minutes

Companion: Outline §4

Weight of this chapter: the most calculation/mechanism-dense chapter in the course: rdt, GBN/SR, TCP sequence numbers/ACK/RTT, flow control, congestion control.

docs.title: 0. Chapter thread (memorize these three sentences first)
docs.text:
1. The transport layer provides process-to-process logical communication; multiplexing/demultiplexing rely on ports (TCP also needs the 4-tuple).
  2. Reliable transfer = ACKs + sequence numbers + timers + retransmission; pipelining (GBN/SR) uses windows to raise utilization.
  3. TCP adds flow control (rwnd) and congestion control (cwnd) on top of reliable transfer; AIMD + slow start is the classic form, CUBIC/QUIC are the modern evolution.

Common question types in this chapter

Question type Typical phrasing What to prepare Calculation stop-and-wait utilization, TCP throughput, RTT estimation Remember formulas + units Mechanism rdt2.0 flaw, GBN/SR windows, three-way handshake Draw the timing/state diagram Analysis Given a loss/delay scenario, ask about retransmission/ACK Reason from “sequence number + timer” Comparison TCP vs UDP, GBN vs SR, flow control vs congestion Make a table Short answer Why the three-way handshake? Why is AIMD fair? Grasp the key reasons

docs.title: 1.1 Position and responsibilities ★
docs.text:
• Network layer: host-to-host; transport layer: process-to-process.
  • Sender: breaks application data into segments, adds the transport-layer header, passes it to the network layer.
  • Receiver: reassembles segments and delivers them to the correct socket by port.
  • The transport layer is implemented only in end systems; routers do not process the transport layer.

docs.title: 1.2 Multiplexing/demultiplexing (mux/demux) ★★
docs.text:
Multiplexing (sender): gather data from multiple sockets, add the header (source/dest port, etc.), pass it to the network layer.

Demultiplexing (receiver): use header fields to deliver the segment to the correct socket.

Protocol Demultiplexing identifier UDP <dest IP, dest port> TCP <source IP, source port, dest IP, dest port> 4-tuple
  • UDP: same dest port but different source → delivered to the same socket.
  • TCP: the 4-tuple uniquely identifies a connection; the same port can have multiple connections.

docs.title: 2.1 Characteristics ★
docs.text:
• Connectionless: no handshaking; each datagram is independent.
  • Unreliable: no guarantee of arrival, order, or non-duplication.
  • No flow control/congestion control: the sender sends at the application's pace.
  • Small overhead, low delay, header is only 8 bytes.
  • Suitable for: DNS, DHCP, SNMP, streaming media, games, the QUIC substrate.

Why use UDP:

  • the application implements reliability/real-time delivery itself;
  • it does not want to be slowed down by TCP's congestion control/retransmission;
  • for short request/response (DNS), the connection-setup cost is not worth it.

docs.title: 2.2 UDP header ★★
docs.text:
0               16              31
+----------------+----------------+
| source port(16)| dest port(16)  |
+----------------+----------------+
| length(16)     | checksum(16)   |
+----------------+----------------+
| data ...                        |
+---------------------------------+
  • Length: header + data (bytes), minimum 8.
  • Checksum: covers the pseudo-header + UDP header + data; the pseudo-header contains the source/dest IP, protocol number, and UDP length.
  • Computation: 16-bit one's complement sum, then complement it; the receiver verifies (all 1s means no checksum, optional in IPv4).

The checksum is very weak: 16 bits, errors may slip through; but better than nothing.

docs.title: 3.1 Interfaces and assumptions
docs.text:
rdt_send(data)        // called from above
udt_send(packet)      // pass to unreliable channel
rdt_rcv(packet)       // receive packet from channel
deliver_data(data)    // deliver to upper layer

Add channel assumptions step by step: reliable → bit errors → packet loss.

docs.title: 3.2 rdt1.0: reliable channel
docs.text:
• Sender: receive data → make packet → send.
  • Receiver: receive packet → extract → deliver.
  • No ACK, sequence number, or timer needed.

docs.title: 3.3 rdt2.0: channel with bit errors ★
docs.text:
• Needs: error detection (checksum), ACK/NAK, retransmission.
  • The sender sends and then waits for ACK/NAK; on NAK or corruption → retransmit.
  • Fatal flaw: the ACK/NAK itself may be corrupted → the sender does not know whether it was “success” or “failure”, so it may send a duplicate.

docs.title: 3.4 rdt2.1: handling garbled ACK/NAK ★
docs.text:
• Add sequence number 0/1 to the data packet.
  • Sender: send the current packet, wait for the corresponding ACK; timeout/corruption → retransmit.
  • Receiver: use the sequence number to detect duplicates; discard duplicates but still send ACK.
  • Twice as many states (wait for ACK0 / ACK1).

docs.title: 3.5 rdt2.2: NAK-free ★
docs.text:
• Uses ACK only; the ACK carries “the next sequence number expected”.
  • Receiver on a correct packet → send ACK (expected seq #); on duplicate/out-of-order → resend the previous ACK.
  • Sender on a duplicate ACK → retransmit the current packet.
  • Same functionality as rdt2.1, but one fewer message type.

docs.title: 3.6 rdt3.0: channels with loss ★★
docs.text:
• Add a timer: start it after sending; if no ACK arrives before the timeout → retransmit.
  • Sequence numbers 0/1; handling:
  • data lost → timeout retransmission;
  • ACK lost → timeout retransmission (receiver discards the duplicate);
  • delayed ACK → possible duplicate, but sequence numbers can handle it.
  • stop-and-wait: send only one packet at a time, then wait for the ACK; simple but extremely low utilization.

docs.title: 3.7 stop-and-wait performance ★★
docs.text:
\[ U_{\text{sender}} = \frac{L/R}{RTT + L/R} \]

Example (slides): 1 Gbps link, 15 ms one-way propagation (RTT=30 ms), 8000-bit packet. - \(\tfrac{L}{R} = \tfrac{8000}{10^9} = 8\ \mu\text{s} = 0.008\ \text{ms}\) - \(U = \tfrac{0.008}{30+0.008} \approx 0.00027\) - That is, the sender is sending data only 0.027% of the time.

Fix: pipelining — allow multiple unacknowledged packets to be in flight at once; utilization increases by a factor of N.

docs.title: 4.1 Go-Back-N (GBN) ★★
docs.text:
Sender

  • Window N: at most N consecutive unacknowledged packets.
  • k-bit sequence numbers; the window slides.
  • Cumulative ACK: ACK(n) means n and all packets before it have been received.
  • One timer: only for the oldest unacknowledged packet; on timeout → retransmit that packet and all subsequent packets in the window.

Receiver

  • Accepts only in order; expects rcv_base.
  • Correct sequence number → deliver, send ACK, rcv_base++.
  • Out-of-order packet → discard (do not buffer), re-ACK the last correctly received packet (may generate duplicate ACKs).

Characteristics: the receiver is simple; losing one packet retransmits the whole window, wasting bandwidth.

docs.title: 4.2 Selective Repeat (SR) ★★
docs.text:
Sender

  • Window N; a separate timer for each packet.
  • Retransmits only the packet that timed out.
  • ACK received → mark that packet as ACKed; the window slides.

Receiver

  • Buffers out-of-order packets; individually ACKs each correctly received packet.
  • Delivers in order; once the missing packet arrives, delivers the buffered consecutive packets together.

Window constraint:

\[ N \le 2^{k-1} \]
  • k is the number of sequence-number bits; the sequence-number space is 2^k, and the window cannot exceed half of it, otherwise “new packet” and “retransmission of an old packet” cannot be distinguished.
  • Example: k=2 (sequence numbers 0..3), N at most 2; with N=3 the receiver will mistake an old packet for a new one.

docs.title: 4.3 GBN vs SR ★★
docs.text: Dimension GBN SR Receiver buffering does not buffer out-of-order packets buffers out-of-order packets ACK cumulative ACK individual ACK Retransmission whole window only the lost packet Timer one (oldest packet) one per packet Window N N ≤ 2^(k-1) Complexity simple complex Applicable few errors / small window many errors / high bandwidth

docs.title: 5.1 Overview ★
docs.text:
• Point-to-point: one sender, one receiver.
  • Reliable, in-order: byte stream.
  • Full duplex: bidirectional data.
  • Connection-oriented: a handshake establishes state.
  • Flow control: rwnd.
  • Congestion control: cwnd.

docs.title: 5.2 TCP segment structure ★★
docs.text:
0               16              31
+----------------+----------------+
| source port(16)| dest port(16)  |
+----------------+----------------+
| sequence number (32)            |
+---------------------------------+
| acknowledgement number (32)     |
+---------------------------------+
|head| not | flag| receive window |
+----+-----+-----+----------------+
| checksum(16)   | urg data ptr   |
+----------------+----------------+
| options (variable length)       |
+---------------------------------+
| data ...                        |
  • Minimum header 20 bytes (no options).
  • Flags: SYN, ACK, FIN, RST, PSH, URG.
  • Sequence number: byte-stream number, not a packet number.
  • Acknowledgement number: the sequence number of the next byte expected (cumulative ACK).

docs.title: 5.3 Sequence numbers and ACKs ★★
docs.text:
• The sender numbers every byte; the sequence number of the segment's first byte goes in Seq.
  • Receiver ACK = next byte expected.
  • Example: send 1000 bytes, Seq=1000; the receiver receives them correctly → ACK=2000.
  • Loss/out-of-order: the receiver re-ACKs the current expected value; the sender sees 3 duplicate ACKs → fast retransmit.

docs.title: 5.4 RTT estimation and timeout ★★
docs.text:
\[ \begin{aligned} \text{EstimatedRTT} &= (1-\alpha)\cdot\text{EstimatedRTT} + \alpha\cdot\text{SampleRTT}, & \alpha &= 0.125\\ \text{DevRTT} &= (1-\beta)\cdot\text{DevRTT} + \beta\cdot|\text{SampleRTT} - \text{EstimatedRTT}|, & \beta &= 0.25\\ \text{TimeoutInterval} &= \text{EstimatedRTT} + 4\cdot\text{DevRTT} \end{aligned} \]
  • EstimatedRTT: the smoothed RTT estimate.
  • DevRTT: RTT deviation (jitter).
  • Timeout = estimate + safety margin; large deviation → longer timeout.
  • Timeout too long → slow reaction; too short → unnecessary retransmissions.

Example: EstimatedRTT=120 ms, DevRTT=10 ms, SampleRTT=100 ms. - new Estimated = 0.875×120 + 0.125×100 = 117.5 ms - new Dev = 0.75×10 + 0.25×|100−120| = 12.5 ms - Timeout = 117.5 + 4×12.5 = 167.5 ms

docs.title: 5.5 TCP sender (simplified) ★
docs.text:
Events:

  1. Application passes data → create segment → start timer → send.
  2. Timeout → retransmit the oldest unACKed segment → restart timer.
  3. ACK received → update window; if there is still unACKed data → restart timer; otherwise stop.

docs.title: 5.6 Fast retransmit ★
docs.text:
• Receiving 3 duplicate ACKs (same acknowledgement number) → treat the segment as lost and retransmit immediately, without waiting for the timeout.
  • Why 3: a small amount of reordering also produces duplicate ACKs; 3 is a compromise that reduces false judgments.

docs.title: 5.7 TCP receiver ACK generation
docs.text: Event Action in-order segment received, all earlier data already ACKed delayed ACK (up to 500 ms) out-of-order segment received immediately send a duplicate ACK (expected seq #) segment that fills the gap received immediate ACK

docs.title: 5.8 Flow control ★★
docs.text:
• Goal: prevent the sender from overflowing the receiver's buffer.
  • The receiver advertises free space in the rwnd (receive window) field of the header.
  • The sender guarantees: \(\text{unACKed data} \le rwnd\).
  • Difference from congestion control:
  • Flow control: receiver-imposed limit (end-to-end).
  • Congestion control: network-imposed limit (global).

docs.title: 5.9 Connection management ★★
docs.text:
Three-way handshake

client → server: SYN, seq=x
server → client: SYN-ACK, seq=y, ack=x+1
client → server: ACK, ack=y+1
  • Goal: synchronize both sides' sequence numbers and confirm both sides' send/receive capability.
  • Why three: to prevent an old duplicate SYN from reaching the server and causing a wrong connection to be established; two is not enough, four is wasteful.

Closing a connection

  • The active closer sends FIN; the peer ACKs; the peer also sends FIN; final ACK.
  • The active closer enters TIME_WAIT and waits 2×MSL, to ensure the final ACK can arrive and old packets disappear.

docs.title: 5.10 Retransmission scenarios
docs.text:
• ACK lost: the sender times out and retransmits; the receiver receives a duplicate → ACKs again.
  • Data lost: timeout / 3 duplicate ACKs → retransmit.
  • Delayed ACK: may cause a “premature timeout”, but sequence numbers/ACKs can recover.

docs.title: 6.1 Costs of congestion ★
docs.text:
• queueing delay increases;
  • buffer overflow → packet loss;
  • retransmissions waste bandwidth;
  • congestion collapse (throughput drops sharply).

Three scenarios:

  1. One router, finite buffers: arrival rate approaches capacity → queueing/loss.
  2. Multiple routers, retransmissions: loss causes retransmissions, which make congestion worse.
  3. Four senders, multi-hop: competing for bandwidth, throughput drops.

docs.title: 6.2 Two approaches
docs.text: Approach Who does it Example End-end end systems infer from observed loss/delay TCP Network-assisted routers provide explicit feedback ECN, ATM ABR

docs.title: 6.3 TCP AIMD ★★
docs.text:
• Additive increase (AI): cwnd += 1 MSS per RTT.
  • Multiplicative decrease (MD): on loss, cwnd = cwnd/2.
  • Sawtooth: probe for available bandwidth → loss → halve → increase again.
  • Fairness: when multiple flows compete, AIMD converges to roughly fair.

docs.title: 6.4 Slow start ★★
docs.text:
• Initially cwnd = 1 MSS.
  • For every ACK received, cwnd += 1 MSS → doubles every RTT (exponential growth).
  • After reaching ssthresh, enter congestion avoidance (linear growth).
  • Timeout: ssthresh = cwnd/2, cwnd = 1, restart slow start.
  • 3 duplicate ACKs: fast retransmit + fast recovery:
  • ssthresh = cwnd/2
  • cwnd = ssthresh (or ssthresh+3)
  • then grow linearly.

Example: initial cwnd=1, ssthresh=8. - Slow start: 1→2→4→8 (3 RTTs). - Congestion avoidance: 9→10→11... - Loss at cwnd=12 (3 dup ACKs): ssthresh=6, cwnd=6, then 7,8,...

docs.title: 6.5 TCP CUBIC ★
docs.text:
• Grows the window with a cubic function (with time as the independent variable):
  • grows slowly near the previous congestion point, fast when far from it;
  • better suited to high-bandwidth, long-delay networks.
  • Linux default; more stable and faster to recover than AIMD.

docs.title: 6.6 Delay-based congestion control
docs.text:
• Measure RTT changes and keep the pipe “just full” without causing loss.
  • Representatives: TCP Vegas; BBR uses bandwidth/RTT estimates.
  • Pros: few losses; cons: may be unfair to loss-based flows.

docs.title: 6.7 ECN (explicit congestion notification)
docs.text:
• Routers mark congestion in the IP header (instead of dropping).
  • The receiver echoes it back in the TCP ACK; the sender slows down.
  • Requires end-to-end support.

docs.title: 6.8 Fairness ★
docs.text:
• Goal: K TCP flows share a bottleneck, each gets about R/K.
  • AIMD tends toward fairness.
  • Factors that break fairness:
  • different RTTs (short RTTs grab more);
  • UDP does not slow down;
  • multiple parallel connections;
  • application-layer unfairness.

docs.title: 6.9 TCP throughput (supplement)
docs.text:
\[ \text{avg throughput} \approx \frac{0.75W}{RTT} \]
  • W is the window size at loss; the average window is about \(\tfrac{3}{4}W\).
  • With loss rate L (Mathis): \(\text{throughput} \approx \tfrac{1.22\cdot\text{MSS}}{RTT\cdot\sqrt{L}}\).
  • High-bandwidth long-delay networks need a large window; the loss rate must be extremely low.

docs.title: 7. QUIC (for awareness)
docs.text:
• An application-layer protocol on top of UDP; the transport layer of HTTP/3.
  • Stream-level multiplexing: loss on one stream does not affect the others (avoids TCP HOL blocking).
  • 0/1-RTT connection establishment: reduces handshake delay.
  • Built-in encryption (TLS 1.3).
  • Connection migration: keeps the connection alive when a phone switches between WiFi/cellular.
  • User-space implementation, easy to iterate quickly.

docs.title: Example 1: stop-and-wait utilization (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: 1 Gbps link, 15 ms one-way propagation, 8000-bit packet. Find the sender utilization of stop-and-wait.

Solution: - \(\tfrac{L}{R} = \tfrac{8000}{10^9} = 8\ \mu\text{s} = 0.008\ \text{ms}\) - \(RTT = 30\ \text{ms}\) - \(U = \tfrac{0.008}{30+0.008} \approx 0.00027\) (0.027%) - Conclusion: pipelining is needed to improve utilization.

docs.title: Example 2: GBN retransmission (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: GBN, N=4, sequence numbers 0..7. Send 0,1,2,3; ACK0 and ACK1 arrive; then send 4,5; packet 2 is lost. What happens when the receiver gets 3,4,5? When does the sender retransmit, and which packets?

Solution: - The receiver expects 2; 3,4,5 all arrive out of order → discard (or buffer, depending on the implementation), duplicate ACK1. - The sender receives duplicate ACK1, but fewer than 3; packet 2's timer times out → retransmit 2,3,4,5 (the whole window). - After receiving 2, the receiver delivers 2,3,4,5 in order and sends ACK5.

docs.title: Example 3: TCP sequence numbers/ACK (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: TCP sends 2000 bytes with Seq=5000; the receiver correctly receives the first 1000 bytes, and the last 1000 bytes are lost. What ACK does the receiver send back? How does the sender react?

Solution: - The receiver receives 5000–5999, expects 6000 → ACK=6000. - Later segments outside 6000–6999 (if any) → duplicate ACK 6000. - The sender receives 3 duplicate ACK 6000 → fast retransmit the segment starting at 6000.

docs.title: Example 4: RTT estimation (8 points)
docs.text:
Question: EstimatedRTT=200 ms, DevRTT=20 ms, SampleRTT=160 ms. Find the new EstimatedRTT, DevRTT, and Timeout.

Solution: - Estimated = 0.875×200 + 0.125×160 = 175 + 20 = 195 ms - Dev = 0.75×20 + 0.25×|160−195| = 15 + 8.75 = 23.75 ms - Timeout = 195 + 4×23.75 = 290 ms

docs.title: Example 5: AIMD (10 points)
docs.text:
Question: cwnd=1, ssthresh=16. Describe slow start up to cwnd=16, then what happens when 3 duplicate ACKs occur at cwnd=20.

Solution: - Slow start: 1→2→4→8→16 (4 RTTs, exponential). - Congestion avoidance: 17,18,19,20 (+1 per RTT). - 3 dup ACKs: ssthresh = 20/2 = 10; cwnd = 10 (fast recovery), then 11,12,... linear growth. - If it were a timeout: ssthresh=10, cwnd=1, restart slow start.

docs.title: Example 6: TCP throughput (6 points)
docs.text:
Question: W=64 KB, RTT=100 ms. Estimate the average throughput.

Solution: - \(\tfrac{0.75\times64\ \text{KB}}{0.1\ \text{s}} = 480\ \text{KB/s} \approx 3.84\ \text{Mbps}\). - If the loss rate is high, the actual value is lower; high bandwidth and long delay need a larger W.

docs.title: 9. Common mistakes (where marks are most often lost)
docs.text: Mistake Correct transport layer = host-to-host the transport layer is process-to-process; the network layer is host-to-host UDP has no checksum UDP has a 16-bit checksum (optional in IPv4, usually enabled) rdt2.0 is already reliable ACK/NAK may be corrupted → it has a fatal flaw the GBN receiver buffers out-of-order packets GBN usually discards out-of-order packets; only SR buffers them the SR window may equal the sequence-number space N ≤ 2^(k-1), otherwise there is ambiguity TCP sequence numbers are packet numbers they are byte-stream numbers ACK means “this sequence number has been received” ACK means “the next byte expected” timeout = 2×RTT use EstimatedRTT + 4×DevRTT 3 duplicate ACKs always mean loss they may also be reordering; 3 is a compromise flow control = congestion control rwnd prevents receiver overflow; cwnd prevents network overload the three-way handshake is for encryption it is for synchronizing sequence numbers and preventing old connections slow start keeps growing exponentially after ssthresh it turns linear AIMD halves the window on loss multiplicative decrease; a timeout may drop it to 1 TCP is always fair RTT/UDP/parallel connections break fairness

docs.title: 10. Self-test (do it first, then check the answers)
docs.text:
1. Difference between the transport layer and the network layer? What do multiplexing/demultiplexing do?
  2. UDP header fields? What does the checksum cover? Why is the protection said to be weak?
  3. Fatal flaw of rdt2.0? How do rdt2.1/2.2 solve it?
  4. How does rdt3.0 handle packet loss? What is the utilization formula for stop-and-wait?
  5. Differences between GBN and SR in window, ACK, retransmission, and buffering?
  6. What is the minimum TCP segment header size? What do the sequence number and acknowledgement number mean?
  7. How does TCP estimate RTT and set the timeout? What do α and β do?
  8. What triggers fast retransmit? Why 3 duplicate ACKs?
  9. Difference between flow control and congestion control? What are rwnd and cwnd?
  10. What is the procedure of the TCP three-way handshake? Why three times?
  11. What are the procedures of AIMD, slow start, and fast recovery? What does CUBIC improve?
  12. What is TCP fairness? Which factors break fairness?
  13. What are the advantages of QUIC over TCP?

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
1. The network layer is host-to-host, the transport layer is process-to-process; mux/demux delivers segments to the correct socket.
  2. Source/dest port, length, checksum; pseudo-header + UDP segment; 16-bit one's complement sum, weak protection.
  3. ACK/NAK may be corrupted; rdt2.1 adds sequence numbers, rdt2.2 uses ACK + expected seq #.
  4. Retransmit on timer timeout; \(U=\tfrac{L/R}{RTT+L/R}\).
  5. GBN: cumulative ACK, one timer, retransmits the whole window, the receiver does not buffer; SR: individual ACK, per-packet timer, retransmits only the lost packet, buffers out-of-order packets.
  6. 20 bytes; Seq is the number of the segment's first byte, ACK is the next byte expected.
  7. Exponential weighted moving average; α smooths SampleRTT, β smooths the deviation; Timeout=EstimatedRTT+4DevRTT.
  8. 3 duplicate ACKs; they show that later packets arrived but the missing packet did not, so the network probably dropped only that one.
  9. Flow control prevents receiver overflow (rwnd), congestion control prevents network overload (cwnd).
  10. SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK; synchronize sequence numbers and prevent old connection requests.
  11. AI adds 1 MSS per RTT, MD halves on loss; slow start grows exponentially to ssthresh; fast recovery follows 3 duplicate ACKs; CUBIC uses a cubic function.
  12. K flows sharing a bottleneck each get about R/K; different RTTs, UDP, and parallel connections break it.
  13. Implemented on top of UDP, stream-level multiplexing, 0/1-RTT, built-in encryption, connection migration.
